initial_presentation: A 20-year-old Malaysian woman presented with Angle Class I bimaxillary protrusion. The treatment aimed to reduce upper- and lower-lip protrusion by retracting the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth. To create space for this retraction, four first premolars were extracted. Following the extractions, a fixed pre-adjusted appliance (0.022 inch × 0.028 inch slot) and 0.016 inch nickel titanium (Ni-Ti) archwire were placed. After initial alignment, canine retraction was started on a 018 special plus Australian wire, using an elastomeric chain applying 150 g of force. After 3 months of upper canine retraction, the right canine had moved 1 mm while the left canine had moved 3 mm. The patient noted that the extraction of the upper right premolar had been difficult and took more time.

A 77-year-old male with a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic right mastoiditis reported to his opticians with complaints of blurred vision and a gradual decrease in visual acuity in both eyes over three to four months. The opticians observed bilateral cataracts and noted a potential left homonymous hemianopia, leading to a referral to the ophthalmology clinic. The ophthalmologist subsequently referred him to the stroke clinic due to the suspected hemianopia. At the stroke clinic, the patient exhibited no other objective deficits except for reduced visual acuity and diminished left-sided visual perception. He was in good clinical condition and remained independent in his activities of daily living.
A 53-year-old female with a history of arterial hypertension presented with bilateral vision blurring for 5 days. She had no prior ocular complaints or neurological or auditory symptoms.

A 5-month-old female child, previously healthy and growing well (weight: 5.3 kg, length: 60 cm, weight/height: -1 SD to -2 SD as per WHO growth chart, head circumference: 40.5 cm), presented with a 6-day history of fever followed by 2 days of rapid breathing.

A 26-year-old male, with no consanguinity, presented with multiple painless swellings on his body for the past 12 years, with no notable family history. The initial swelling appeared in the sacral region and gradually increased to a size of 20 cm × 15 cm × 10 cm. Over time, additional swellings emerged in various locations, including the buttocks, extensor aspects of the elbows and knees, and on the hands and feet. These swellings ranged in size from 2 cm × 2 cm on the dorsum of the hands to 15 cm × 10 cm on the buttocks. Upon examination, the swellings were firm, non-tender, mobile, and showed no skin changes.

A 30-year-old female presented with a firm, non-painful area on the right ear lobule. The back part of this skin area showed a 10-mm oval macule with a pronounced steel-blue color, beneath which a small nodule could be felt. The patient recalled a previous local inflammatory reaction caused by a silver earring 25 years ago.

Patient 1 is a 37-year-old male who first visited our clinic at the age of 8 years in 1989. His clinical records up to 1992 were not retained, but a brief summary indicated that he had nystagmus since birth. He was previously noted to have retinitis pigmentosa and hyperopia through clinical examination at the age of 7 at another clinic. Upon his first visit to our clinic, his eyes did not shift in the primary position, and hyperopia and color blindness were detected. Fundus examination was grossly normal. According to the oldest detailed clinical data from 1992, his eye position indicated orthophoria, but horizontal nystagmus was evident, and he reported photophobia.

The patient is a male infant from a consanguineous Saudi family, consisting of two healthy parents and five children (one affected male, two healthy males, one healthy female, and one deceased female). The patient presented with severe coarctation or interrupted aortic arch, patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, gastroesophageal reflux, and glaucoma. He received treatment at the Department of Pediatric Cardiology, King Abdulaziz Medical City, Ministry of National Guard Health Affairs, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The deceased sister exhibited similar clinical features. One male sibling and the parents were carriers of the same genetic variant, while the other two children had no genetic abnormalities.

A 41-year-old man was referred for cardiology consultation for assessment of dextrocardia. His medical history included recurrent pneumonia during childhood and normal growth, with no cardiovascular symptoms. Physical examination revealed he was in good general condition, with clear lungs and no cardiac murmur.

A 62-year-old male from India visited the orthopedics department due to a progressively worsening low back ache. He reported no other symptoms, and his bowel and bladder functions were normal. There was no history of trauma, and the patient appeared healthy and well-nourished. Physical examination revealed no tenderness in the pelvic bones, and neurological examination showed no motor deficits. A whole body bone scan was conducted to investigate potential skeletal issues.
